sentence: Treatments said to rejuvenate cells are usually judged by a single score that falls when cells look younger. But such a score shows only which way cells moved, not where they ended up: it also falls when cells simply stop looking old, for example by drifting toward a different cell type, without becoming any more like young cells. We ask a more direct question: after treatment, are the cells closer to young cells of the same type than they were before? In skin fibroblasts from a 96-year-old donor that were partially reprogrammed (Lu et al.), the published aging score fell well below the level of a 22-year-old donor's untreated cells, which looks like strong rejuvenation. Yet the same cells ended about twice as far from the young donor's cells as they started, even when judged only by the genes that make up that score. The same was true with other published aging genes, with all genes, with hundreds of randomly chosen gene sets, and with an age score we built that follows donor age across several independent cohorts. Our measure does register cells getting closer when young cells are mixed into old ones, so it can see real rejuvenation when it happens, and the result is not the two donors' cells simply becoming more alike. A falling aging score therefore cannot tell rejuvenation apart from cells moving away from their old state in some other direction. We provide a frozen age score, young reference points and code for measuring distance to young cells instead.

Lu et al. use a mesenchymal-drift (MD) signature, the HALLMARK epithelial-mesenchymal transition gene set augmented with SNAI1, ZEB1, ZEB2, TWIST1 and TWIST2 (205 genes), as their readout of aging, and report that it falls when aged fibroblasts are partially reprogrammed. Their dataset GSE297234 is an OSKM reprogramming time course in dermal fibroblasts from a 96-year-old donor (GM00731) and a 22-year-old donor (GM23815), sampled at days 0, 3, 7 and 10. It is unusual among rejuvenation datasets in containing young cells of the same type, on the same platform, in the same experiment, which is what makes the question in this paper answerable. Cell states were labelled with the published state signatures (Methods). The population tested is the aged donor's partially reprogrammed cells (5,832 cells). They are overwhelmingly day-3 cells (5,220 of them), assayed while OSKM is still being expressed; this is the population the source paper treats as rejuvenated. Donors are never pooled, and the 22-year-old donor is a contrast, not a replicate.

We scored MD per cell with a reimplementation of the published algorithm (Methods), scoring both donors against the same control genes so that their scores are comparable. The score behaves as reported. In the aged donor it falls from 0.515 (95% CI 0.514 to 0.517) in day-0 fibroblasts to 0.158 (0.153 to 0.162) in partially reprogrammed cells, and continues downward through early pluripotency (0.147) to pluripotency (0.022). The relevant comparison is the difference between the two donors' day-0 fibroblasts, which is what 74 years of donor age look like on this scale: 0.046 (0.043 to 0.049). The drop on partial reprogramming is 7.7 times that difference (95% CI 7.3 to 8.2). Read as an age readout, the 96-year-old's partially reprogrammed cells are far younger than the 22-year-old's actual cells (Figure 1A).

Part of the reason is a property of the ruler itself. Its score is anticorrelated with distance from its own training distribution: across 22 pseudobulks in the reprogramming dataset (one per donor, cell-state cluster and timepoint, with at least 20 cells), Spearman ρ between nearest-neighbour distance to the GTEx training donors and the frozen score is −0.625 (95% CI −0.834 to −0.320; Figure 5B), and the same sign holds within each donor separately (−0.78 and −0.81). Cells far outside the training data are scored as young. Because distance and reprogramming state move together here, this correlation cannot by itself separate an extrapolation artefact from genuine change, but it does show that a low score cannot be taken at face value.

The ruler is a ridge regression of donor chronological age on z-scored gene expression, fit through the n × n Gram matrix, and frozen with its coefficients and its training mean and standard deviation before any evaluation. The regularisation parameter was selected over the grid 0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 10, 30, 100, 300, 1000, 3000, 10000 by minimising a leave-one-out residual sum of squares computed from the hat-matrix diagonal, not by grouped cross-validation. The frozen fibroblast ruler stores alpha = 0.01, the smallest value on the grid, so a smaller optimum cannot be excluded. The frozen fibroblast vector is the ridge coefficient vector, unit-normalised and sign-aligned so that the score increases with age. Transfers within GTEx use the full prediction (training mean age plus the ridge coefficients applied to the z-scored profile), which is in years. The external cohorts and all reprogramming analyses use the frozen unit-length score, which orders samples identically but has no intercept or scale and is not in years. Within-site fibroblast cross-validation, grouped by sequencing batch with up to five folds, reports ρ but does not choose alpha. The ruler was never refit on any evaluation cohort.

The regularisation parameter was selected over the grid 0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 10, 30, 100, 300, 1000, 3000, 10000 by minimising a leave-one-out residual sum of squares computed from the hat-matrix diagonal, not by grouped cross-validation. The frozen fibroblast ruler stores alpha = 0.01, the smallest value on the grid, so a smaller optimum cannot be excluded. The frozen fibroblast vector is the ridge coefficient vector, unit-normalised and sign-aligned so that the score increases with age. Transfers within GTEx use the full prediction (training mean age plus the ridge coefficients applied to the z-scored profile), which is in years. The external cohorts and all reprogramming analyses use the frozen unit-length score, which orders samples identically but has no intercept or scale and is not in years. Within-site fibroblast cross-validation, grouped by sequencing batch with up to five folds, reports ρ but does not choose alpha. The ruler was never refit on any evaluation cohort.

Analysis unit in the fibroblast atlas. The atlas's donor field holds one identifier per sequencing sample in several constituent studies. Each identifier was traced to its source study and the original author's donor identifier, and pseudobulk scores were averaged within each person before any correlation, permutation or bootstrap, giving 65 donors (64 after dropping pseudobulks with fewer than 30 cells, which gave the same conclusion). Seeds and resampling settings were unchanged.

sentence: For a displacement d from an origin pseudobulk toward a target direction v we report three quantities. Cosine alignment is d·v / (‖d‖ ‖v‖). Progress along the axis is d·v / ‖v‖², which equals 0 at the origin and 1 at the target. The change in distance is ‖z_S − z_target‖ − ‖z_origin − z_target‖, so a positive value means the state ended farther from the target. The sideways component is ‖d − progress·v‖ / ‖v‖, in units of the axis length. In the same-platform test, where the axis ends at the target, final distance divided by starting distance equals √((1 − progress)² + sideways²), so a state ends closer only if it falls inside the unit circle drawn in Figures 1B and 2.

All nulls use 200 draws and an empirical p-value of (exceedances + 1) / 201. Three constructions appear, and they are not interchangeable. A donor-label permutation shuffles donor age within the training bank, holding the expression matrix fixed, and is the null for every transfer statistic. A gene-permutation null shuffles the entries of the frozen target direction across genes, and tests whether a cosine is larger than for a direction with the same coefficient distribution. An anchor null rebuilds the young-minus-old direction from equal-size random splits of all GTEx fibroblast donors, ignoring age, and tests whether an alignment is specifically with age rather than with any donor contrast.

Confidence intervals are 200-draw percentile bootstraps at the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. The resampling unit is the donor for transfer statistics and the cell for displacement statistics. Paired comparisons recompute both quantities on the same resampled donors, so that the interval is on the difference rather than on two separate intervals. Any interval that does not contain its own point estimate is flagged invalid and is not used as a gate; this happens for distance intervals in the high-dimensional displacement tests and is reported at each occurrence.

No test is interpreted until a control has recovered a known effect, and the controls are rebuilt inside each gene space rather than carried over from the full space. Two kinds are used. In the same-platform test, synthetic mixtures combine known fractions of young day-0 cells into aged day-0 cells at fixed total cell count; the control passes if progress increases monotonically with the mixing fraction, the interval on progress at the highest fraction excludes zero, and the change in distance at that fraction is negative. The zero-mixture point is reported as the noise floor and is not subtracted. In the GTEx-anchored test, five folds displace held-out old donors toward the training fold's young centroid; the bar was every fold cosine above 0.5, and the observed minimum was 0.615 in all genes, 0.733 in the MD genes and 0.681 in the age genes.

sentence: Supplementary Note 1. Young defined by GTEx donors

Anchors were the mean expression of the GTEx reference donors aged 20 to 39 (n = 113) and 60 to 79 (n = 231), with the 40 to 59 bins excluded. In all genes, the aged donor's partially reprogrammed displacement is almost orthogonal to the young-minus-old axis (cosine +0.077). That small alignment survives a gene-permutation null (p = 0.005) but not a null in which GTEx donors are split at random ignoring age (p = 0.39), so it is not specifically an age alignment. The cells end farther from the young centroid (+9.4) and farther from the old centroid (+10.9): they recede from both. A five-fold positive control, in which held-out old GTEx donors are displaced toward the young centroid, gave fold cosines of 0.615 to 0.874, above the bar of 0.5, so the statistic registers a genuine approach when one occurs (Supplementary Figure S1D); the control also passes in the MD genes (0.733 to 0.895) and the age genes (0.681 to 0.895).

The GTEx-anchored distances are therefore dominated by the platform gap, and the control does not show that a partial approach would be visible across that gap. This is why the main test uses a young target measured in the same experiment.

Donors are never pooled; the 22-year-old donor is a contrast, not a replicate.

With the roles of the donors reversed, the young donor's partially reprogrammed cells do not move toward the aged donor at all in all genes (progress −0.057, 95% CI −0.063 to −0.054), giving a clear asymmetry (+0.732, CI +0.724 to +0.740). The forward movement is therefore not symmetric mutual convergence. But it is also not obviously age: the aged-to-young donor axis is itself nearly orthogonal to the GTEx donor-age axis (cosine 0.039), so with one donor at each age we cannot separate age from everything else that differs between two cell lines, including proliferative state and culture history. The test can, and does, say that the cells did not approach the young line.
